narration: The stock market looks like a fair auction. Millions of buyers and sellers, a transparent price, everyone playing by the same rules. For most of us, most of the time, that's true.
But underneath, there's a whole hidden menu of tricks designed to tilt that game before you ever place a bet. Fake demand, fake supply, fake information — all quietly rigging the price.
Some of these tricks are ancient. Some are brand new and run by algorithms in millionths of a second. All of them have one goal: to separate you from your money.
The umbrella term is market manipulation — when someone intentionally alters the supply or demand of a security to influence its price.
And a fair price only means something if three things are honest: real supply, real demand, and real information. Every scam in this video is just an attack on one of those three.
It is illegal, it is everywhere, and most of its victims never even realize a game was being played on them.
So let's run the numbers on the most common ways scammers rig the market — and how to spot them.
heading: How Scammers Rig the Stock Market

narration: Start with the most famous trick of all — the one Hollywood made a movie about.
heading: Pump and Dump

narration: A pump and dump artificially inflates the price of an owned stock through false and misleading positive statements — the pump — so the scammer can sell high.
The recipe is simple. First, quietly buy a huge pile of some tiny, cheap stock almost nobody is watching. You now own most of it, dirt cheap.
Then, hype it relentlessly. Hot tips, breathless messages, fake news of a 'can't-miss' opportunity. Excited new buyers pile in, and the price rockets up.
And at the peak — while the crowd is euphoric and buying — the scammer quietly dumps their entire stack. The price collapses, and everyone who believed the hype is left holding the wreckage.
caption: pump the hype, dump on the crowd

narration: Social media turbocharged this. A coordinated crowd in a chat room can now pump a stock in hours, with coordinated 'to the moon' hype — and someone at the top is always quietly selling into it.

label: JORDAN BELFORT
caption: the 'Wolf of Wall Street'
narration: The most infamous practitioner is Jordan Belfort — the 'Wolf of Wall Street' — who ran exactly this scam on cheap stocks and was convicted of fraud for it.
His weapon was the boiler room — an outbound call center selling questionable investments by telephone, using high-pressure, dishonest sales tactics.
These scams are a century old. In the 1920s, shady 'bucket shops' let people bet on stock prices that the shop itself secretly controlled — the original rigged game.

Rooms full of slick salespeople cold-call strangers, pushing worthless 'penny stocks' with scripted urgency. 'It's moving right now — you have to buy today.' It's theater, engineered to switch off your caution.
Today the boiler room has gone digital. The cold call became the group chat, the spam text, the influencer 'alert,' and the too-good-to-be-true direct message. Same scam, bigger reach.
The next trick is invisible to the human eye — it happens in the machines.
heading: Spoofing

narration: Spoofing is a disruptive algorithmic trading tactic. Spoofers feign interest in trading, creating an illusion of the demand and supply of the traded asset.
Here's how it works. A trader places a giant order to buy — making everyone think big demand has arrived — but they never intend to actually complete it.
Other traders and algorithms see the fake wall of demand and rush in. The price ticks up — and the instant it does, the spoofer cancels the fake order and sells into the buyers they just tricked.
caption: fake orders that vanish before they fill

narration: It happens in milliseconds, thousands of times a day. You'd never see it. But regulators have fined banks and traders hundreds of millions of dollars for exactly this.
And the fines are staggering. In 2020, one major bank paid about nine hundred and twenty million dollars to settle spoofing charges — the biggest penalty of its kind.
A close cousin fakes something else entirely: how much a stock is even being traded.
heading: Wash Trading

narration: Wash trading is manipulation where an entity simultaneously sells and buys the same instrument — creating a false impression of market activity.
Basically, you trade with yourself. Buy and sell the same thing back and forth, generating tons of fake volume to make a dead stock look hot and exciting — luring in real buyers.
caption: trading with yourself to fake volume

narration: It's especially rampant in lightly-regulated corners, where 'trending' and 'high volume' are exactly the signals naive investors chase. The activity is real; the interest behind it is a complete fiction.

title: A century of market rigging
narration: This is a very old story. Bucket shops in the 1920s. Ivan Boesky's insider ring in the 80s. Belfort's boiler room in the 90s. The flash crash in 2010. And record spoofing fines in 2020.
The next one doesn't fake demand — it fakes the story, to crash a price on purpose.
heading: Short and Distort

narration: Short and distort is securities fraud where investors short sell a stock and then spread negative rumors to drive the price down.

One important distinction. Honest short selling — betting a stock will fall — is legal and useful. Short sellers helped expose frauds like Enron. The crime isn't the bet. It's deliberately spreading lies to force it true.
It's the evil twin of the pump and dump. Instead of hyping a stock you own, you bet against a stock — then spread scary lies about the company to make your bet pay off.
Pump or distort, the engine is identical: control the story, and you can move the price — regardless of what the company is actually worth.
Now the classic that needs no fake orders at all — just a secret.
heading: Insider Trading

narration: Insider trading is trading a company's stock based on material, nonpublic information — knowing something market-moving before everyone else does.

label: RAJ RAJARATNAM
caption: hedge-fund insider ring
narration: In one of the biggest cases ever, hedge-fund manager Raj Rajaratnam ran a vast insider-trading network — and was caught on wiretaps, then sentenced to eleven years in prison.
Imagine knowing a company will be bought out tomorrow at double the price. Buy today, and it's free money — stolen from the person on the other side who didn't have the secret.

label: MARTHA STEWART
caption: a small trade, a big symbol
narration: Even a relatively small, well-timed sale can bring you down. Martha Stewart famously served prison time in a case tied to suspiciously-timed trading — proof that nobody is too famous to be caught.

label: MICHAEL MILKEN
caption: the 1980s junk-bond scandal
narration: The 1980s were the golden age of this. Financier Michael Milken, the 'junk bond king,' sat at the center of a vast insider scandal — and was convicted of securities violations.

It's hard to detect, because it hides inside perfectly normal-looking trades. But when regulators catch it, the prison sentences are long — because it strikes at the market's one essential promise: a level playing field.
Catching it takes serious firepower: wiretaps, informants, and software that flags a suspiciously perfect trade placed just before big news. Insiders feel invisible — right up until they aren't.
The next trick is quieter, faster, and may be happening to your trades right now.
heading: Front Running

narration: Front running is trading to capitalize on advance, nonpublic knowledge of a large pending transaction that will move the price.

Say a broker sees a huge client order about to hit. If they quickly buy for themselves first, then let the big order push the price up, they pocket the difference — by jumping ahead of their own customer.
caption: jump ahead of the client's order

narration: In the modern market, the fastest computers do a legal-grey version of this at light speed — spotting your order and darting ahead of it in microseconds to skim a tiny slice, millions of times a day.
This is the world of the book 'Flash Boys': high-frequency firms paying for a head start, then racing ahead of ordinary orders through hidden venues called 'dark pools.'
And when enough of these machines interact at once, they can break the whole market in an instant.
heading: The Flash Crash

narration: Ever wonder why your trading app is 'free'? Often it sells your orders to big trading firms — a practice called payment for order flow. You're not the customer; your order is the product.
On May 6th, 2010, the US market suffered a trillion-dollar 'flash crash' — a staggering plunge that lasted only about thirty-six minutes.

In minutes, major stocks lost almost all their value, then bounced back. Investigators later tied part of it to a trader spoofing fake orders — a single manipulator helping tip a cascade of panicking algorithms.
caption: algorithms crash it in seconds

narration: It was a terrifying glimpse of how fragile a machine-driven market can be — and how a little manipulation, at the wrong moment, can ripple into chaos.
There's an even older trick: cornering a market. In 1980, two brothers tried to buy up almost all the world's silver to control the price — before the whole scheme collapsed on them spectacularly.
So if the market is this riggable, why isn't it total anarchy?
heading: The Watchdogs

narration: The honest answer: most of the time, it mostly works. Regulators run huge surveillance systems, scanning for odd patterns, and the penalties — fines and prison — are real deterrents.
And regulators now pay for help. Whistleblowers who report serious fraud can collect a slice of the fines — turning insiders' own colleagues into a small army of watchers.
But enforcement is a step behind the scammers, especially in new, fast, or lightly-regulated markets. The rigging never fully stops — it just moves to wherever the watchdogs aren't yet looking.
The newest frontier is crypto and finfluencers. Lightly regulated tokens and paid-for 'alerts' have revived every old trick at once — pump-and-dumps and wash trades, running wide open, all day.
Which means your best protection isn't the regulator. It's you.
heading: How to Protect Yourself

narration: Rule one: treat every hot tip as a red flag. If a stranger online, a group chat, or a slick caller is urging you to buy some obscure stock right now, you are probably the dump, not the winner.
And watch for the magic phrase: 'guaranteed returns.' No honest investment can promise that. The moment you hear it, you are almost certainly being set up as someone's exit.

memeTop: buy the stock a DM hyped
memeBottom: be the one left holding it
narration: The people pumping a stock to you are not your friends. By the time the tip reaches you, you're usually the last buyer they need.
Rule two: avoid tiny, illiquid penny stocks. Manipulation thrives where a stock is cheap, obscure, and easy to push around. The big, boring, heavily-traded stuff is far harder to rig.
So keep the two worlds straight. Real investing is slow, diversified, and boring. Manipulation is fast, concentrated, and thrilling. If it feels like a thrilling tip, it's probably the trap.
Rule three: distrust urgency. Every one of these scams needs you to act fast, before you think. Real investing is boring and slow — the panic button is the manipulator's favorite tool.

And rule four: own broad, diversified funds instead of chasing individual 'winners.' It's remarkably hard to manipulate an entire index — and nearly impossible to pump a whole market onto one person's bags.
One more: only ever use a properly regulated broker, and check it. A huge share of outright scams start by luring you onto a slick but completely fake 'trading platform.'
So let's total up the rigging.
heading: The Final Math

narration: Pump-and-dumps fake demand. Wash trades fake volume. Spoofing fakes orders. Short-and-distort fakes the story. Insiders cheat with secrets. And front-runners cut the line.
Every single one is a way to fake supply, demand, or information — the three things a fair price is supposed to be built from. Rig any of them, and you've rigged the price.

narration: And yes, sometimes the crowd flips the game. In 2021, an army of small traders squeezed big funds that had shorted a struggling retailer — a wild reminder that manipulation can run in every direction.
And the deepest cost isn't any single scam. It's trust. A market only works when people believe the price is real — and every rig chips away at the foundation the whole thing stands on.
So the next time a stock 'mysteriously' triples on a tip you got in a message, you'll know exactly which game is being played — and you'll know not to be the one holding the bag.
